questions.q: A 35-year-old man from Kerala presents with sudden-onset high fever, arthralgia, and multiple erythematous nodules on his extensor surfaces. He was diagnosed with lepromatous leprosy 6 months ago and is on MDT. The nodules are tender and some have ulcerated. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: ENL (Type 2 lepra reaction) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It presents with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic symptoms. It is an immune complex (Type III hypersensitivity) mediated reaction. Type 1 reaction occurs in borderline leprosy with nerve involvement and silent skin changes.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions and flaccid bullae over the trunk and back. Nikolsky sign is positive. Biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis. Immunofluorescence reveals IgG deposition in an intercellular pattern. The autoantigen in this condition is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is characterized by antibodies against Desmoglein 3 (mucosal type) and both Desmoglein 3 and 1 (mucocutaneous type). Desmoglein 3 is predominantly expressed in the oral mucosa and lower epidermis, explaining the suprabasal acantholysis. BP180 is the target in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with photosensitive facial rash, discoid lesions, Raynaud's phenomenon, and alopecia. Her ANA is positive with anti-dsDNA antibodies. Which skin finding is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: The butterfly (malar) rash of SLE is characteristic, involving both cheeks and the nasal bridge while sparing the nasolabial folds. It is photosensitive and does not scar. Discoid lesions can occur in DLE (without systemic involvement) and are less specific for SLE. Livedo reticularis and palpable purpura can occur in various conditions.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child is admitted with high fever, diffuse erythema, and large, easily ruptured bullae filled with clear fluid. The skin peels off in sheets on gentle pressure (Nikolsky sign positive). The underlying mechanism is:
opts: Immune complex deposition at the dermoepidermal junction
questions.exp: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B from Staphylococcus aureus, which cleave desmoglein 1 in the superficial epidermis (stratum granulosum). This is distinct from TEN, where cell-mediated cytotoxicity causes full-thickness epidermal necrosis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old student presents with multiple hypopigmented macules on the trunk with fine scaling that becomes more apparent on stretching the skin (Besnier's sign positive). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur (also M. globosa). The organism produces azelaic acid which inhibits tyrosinase, causing hypopigmentation. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence due to pityriacitrin production.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child develops painful oral ulcers on the buccal mucosa and tongue, along with vesicles on palms, soles, and buttocks. The child is febrile with poor oral intake. The most common causative agent is:
questions.exp: Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD) is most commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16, though Enterovirus 71 causes more severe neurological complications. Characteristic features include oral ulcers and acral vesicles. HSV causes herpetic gingivostomatitis without palmoplantar involvement.

questions.q: A 26-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated, clean-based ulcer on the glans penis that appeared 3 weeks ago. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, rubbery, and non-tender. Dark field microscopy of exudate shows motile spirochetes. The stage of syphilis is:
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents with a painless indurated chancre at the site of inoculation, with regional non-tender lymphadenopathy (Hunterian bubo). Dark field microscopy demonstrates Treponema pallidum. Secondary syphilis appears 6-8 weeks after the chancre and includes mucocutaneous lesions, condyloma lata, and systemic features.

questions.q: A 62-year-old male smoker presents with a slowly enlarging, pearly nodule on the nose with raised rolled borders and central telangiectasia. There is central ulceration. The most common histological subtype is:
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common subtype (60-80%), presenting as a pearly, flesh-colored nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasia, often with central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Morpheaform BCC appears as a scar-like plaque and has the worst prognosis. Superficial BCC appears as an erythematous scaly plaque.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy is started on dapsone. After 2 weeks, he develops acute hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia. This adverse effect is related to:
opts: Dapsone is oxidized to hydroxylamine metabolite
Direct toxicity to bone marrow progenitors
questions.exp: Dapsone is metabolized by N-hydroxylation to hydroxylamine derivatives, which cause dose-dependent hemolysis and methemoglobinemia. Patients with G6PD deficiency are at higher risk. The drug's mechanism of action (inhibition of dihydropteroate synthase) is separate from its toxicity profile.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops a vesicular eruption on an erythematous base along the T4 dermatome after breast cancer chemotherapy. The pathophysiology involves:
opts: Reactivation of latent VZV from dorsal root ganglion
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to chemotherapy
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) that remained latent in dorsal root ganglia after primary chickenpox infection. Immunosuppression (from chemotherapy, HIV, aging) triggers reactivation. The dermatomal distribution is the hallmark feature.

questions.q: A patient with borderline tuberculoid leprosy on MDT develops sudden painful swelling of the skin lesions with acute neuritis causing wrist drop. There is no fever or systemic symptoms. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) occurs in borderline leprosy and is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It presents with inflamed skin lesions and acute neuritis. Treatment is prednisolone (40-60 mg/day) tapered over at least 6 months. MDT should NOT be stopped. Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2 reaction).

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with tense bullae over normal-appearing skin and urticarial plaques. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister with eosinophilic infiltrate. Direct IF shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by autoantibodies against BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1). BP180 is a hemidesmosomal protein. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Tense bullae and eosinophilia distinguish it from pemphigus. Type VII collagen is the target in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness and heliotrope discoloration of eyelids with periorbital edema. She has Gottron's papules over the metacarpophalangeal joints. Which antibody is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis is characterized by inflammatory myopathy plus skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, shawl sign). Anti-Mi-2 is most specific for classical dermatomyositis. Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl tRNA synthetase) is associated with antisynthetase syndrome (ILD, mechanic's hands, fever). Anti-Scl-70 is for scleroderma.

questions.q: A diabetic patient presents with painful ulceration and gangrenous changes over the lower limb. The wound reveals bluish-green pus with characteristic fruity odor. Gram stain shows gram-negative rods. The organism responsible is:
questions.exp: Ecthyma gangrenosum is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, typically in immunocompromised or diabetic patients. Classic features include painless macule progressing to hemorrhagic bulla then gangrenous ulcer. Bluish-green pus with fruity (grape-like) odor is characteristic of Pseudomonas.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer from Tamil Nadu presents with warty cauliflower-like plaques on the foot. Biopsy shows muriform (sclerotic) bodies. The causative organisms include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (melanized) fungi including Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Phialophora verrucosa, and Cladophialophora carrionii. Histopathology shows characteristic muriform (sclerotic, medlar) bodies - brown, thick-walled cells with horizontal and vertical septae. Sporothrix schenckii causes sporotrichosis, not chromoblastomycosis.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with multiple pearly white umbilicated papules 2-5mm in size over the trunk and extremities. The lesions are asymptomatic. The causative agent belongs to which family?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by the Molluscipoxvirus, a member of the Poxviridae family. The characteristic finding is the central umbilication and Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies on cytology. It is transmitted by direct contact. In HIV patients, giant mollusca (>1cm) can occur.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with painful genital ulcers, multiple in number with undermined edges. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, matted, and tender with overlying skin erythema (bubo). Gram stain shows 'school of fish' pattern. The organism is:
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. It presents with painful, soft, multiple ulcers with undermined ragged edges and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain shows gram-negative rods in a 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern. Contrast with syphilitic chancre (painless, single, indurated).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with HIV (CD4 50 cells/μL) presents with violaceous papules and nodules on the skin, hard palate, and lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows spindle cells with vascular slits and hemosiderin deposition. The causative agent is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV patients is caused by HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, KSHV). It is an AIDS-defining illness. Classic presentation includes violaceous vascular tumors. Histology shows spindle cell proliferation with vascular slits, lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, and hemosiderin. Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) can mimic it but has neutrophilic infiltrate.

questions.q: A patient on methotrexate for psoriasis develops oral ulcers, macrocytic anemia, and elevated liver enzymes after 3 months. The mechanism of methotrexate's anti-psoriatic action is:
opts: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase leading to decreased DNA synthesis
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), depleting tetrahydrofolate and impairing DNA synthesis, thereby reducing keratinocyte proliferation. It also has anti-inflammatory effects. Side effects include mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and myelosuppression. Leucovorin rescue and folic acid supplementation reduce toxicity.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic, grouped vesicles on extensor elbows, knees, and buttocks. She has a history of celiac disease. Biopsy with DIF shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. The treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely pruritic blistering disorder associated with celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy). DIF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae (pathognomonic). Treatment is dapsone for immediate symptom relief and lifelong gluten-free diet for the underlying condition. Linear IgA disease shows linear IgA deposition.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive skin hardening over the face and hands, with Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, and calcinosis. Anti-Scl-70 antibodies are positive. The histological finding in the dermis is:
opts: Dense homogeneous collagen bundles replacing fat and adnexae
Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with mucin deposition
questions.exp: Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) shows dense homogeneous collagen bundles in the reticular dermis, replacing normal structures including adnexa and subcutaneous fat. There is obliterative endarteritis of small vessels. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and ILD. Anti-centromere antibody is for limited SSc (CREST syndrome).

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic patient presents with well-demarcated brownish-red patches in bilateral axillae with coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. KOH mount is negative. The treatment is:
questions.exp: Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. Classic features include coral-red fluorescence on Wood's lamp (due to coproporphyrin III production) and negative KOH mount. It affects intertriginous areas. Treatment is topical or oral erythromycin. Topical clindamycin, fusidic acid, or azole antifungals are alternatives.

questions.q: A gardener presents with painless nodule on the hand that broke down to form an ulcer, followed by new nodules appearing along the lymphatics ascending the arm. KOH shows cigar-shaped yeast forms. The route of infection is:
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis (rose thorn disease) is caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus. Infection occurs by traumatic inoculation (thorns, splinters). The lymphocutaneous form (most common) shows ascending nodules along lymphatics. At 37°C it forms cigar-shaped yeast (tissue form); at 25°C it forms hyphae with conidia (environmental form).

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man develops disseminated varicella with vesicular eruptions at all stages including hemorrhagic lesions, hepatitis, and pneumonitis. CD4 count is 80 cells/μL. The appropriate management is:
questions.exp: Disseminated VZV in immunocompromised patients (HIV, transplant) requires IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8h for 7-10 days) due to risk of life-threatening complications (encephalitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis). Oral acyclovir is insufficient for visceral involvement. VZIG is for post-exposure prophylaxis, not treatment of active disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy with matted nodes, a groove sign (groove of Poupart's ligament between femoral and inguinal nodes). He gives history of a transient genital ulcer that healed spontaneously. The causative agent serotypes are:
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. Classic stages: primary (transient painless ulcer), secondary (inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy with groove sign - Greenblatt sign), tertiary (lymphedema, esthiomene). Serovars D-K cause non-gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis without lymphadenopathy.

questions.q: A 60-year-old patient presents with erythematous patches that evolved to raised plaques over years. Skin biopsy shows Pautrier's microabscesses, epidermotropism, and atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei. The malignant cell type is:
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF), the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, involves malignant CD4+ T cells with a Th2 cytokine profile. Pautrier's microabscesses (collections of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis) and cerebriform (Lutzner) cells are characteristic. Sézary syndrome is the leukemic variant with CD4+CD7-CD26- cells.

questions.q: A 17-year-old girl with severe nodulocystic acne is started on isotretinoin. Which monitoring parameter is most critical before and during therapy?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). The iPLEDGE program mandates two negative pregnancy tests before initiation and monthly during therapy for females of childbearing potential. Two forms of contraception must be used. Lipid panel and LFTs are monitored but pregnancy testing is the most critical safety requirement.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with indeterminate leprosy has a single hypopigmented patch with loss of sensation. Slit skin smear is negative. According to WHO classification, what is the recommended treatment?
questions.exp: Single lesion paucibacillary (SLPB) leprosy with only one skin lesion and no nerve involvement is treated with single-dose ROM (Rifampicin 600mg + Ofloxacin 400mg + Minocycline 100mg). PB-MDT (6 months) is for 2-5 lesions, MB-MDT (12 months) for 6+ lesions. This WHO classification simplifies treatment in field conditions.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man with a 5-year history of chronic plaque psoriasis develops joint pain and swelling in DIP joints with nail pitting. His PASI score is 22. The most appropriate biologic therapy targeting IL-17A is:
questions.exp: Secukinumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody against IL-17A, approved for moderate-severe plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Ixekizumab also targets IL-17A. IL-17A is a key cytokine in psoriasis pathogenesis. For psoriatic arthritis with DIP involvement, IL-17 inhibitors have excellent efficacy for both skin and joint disease.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with multiple verrucous papules on palms and fingers, some with thrombosed capillaries appearing as black dots on the surface. Dermoscopy shows red-dotted papillary loops. The causative HPV types for common warts are:
questions.exp: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are caused by HPV types 2 and 4 (also type 1 for plantar warts). HPV 6 and 11 cause anogenital condylomata acuminata (low-risk). HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic types causing cervical and anogenital carcinomas. HPV 5 and 8 are associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis.

questions.q: A patient presents with a rapidly growing, well-demarcated, flesh-colored nodule with central keratin-filled crater on the cheek. The lesion appeared 6 weeks ago and measured 2.5 cm. Histology shows a cup-shaped epidermal invagination filled with keratin and atypical squamous cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing, self-involuting tumor of follicular origin. Classic features: rapid growth over weeks, dome-shaped nodule with central keratin plug, histologically cup-shaped architecture. Most authorities now consider it a variant of well-differentiated SCC. Spontaneous involution over 3-6 months distinguishes it clinically from SCC.
